questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four defining properties of standard Brownian motion?
options: Independent increments
W_t − W_s ~ N(0, t−s)
Paths are differentiable everywhere
questions.explain: Standard Brownian motion has continuous but nowhere-differentiable paths — the exact opposite of 'differentiable everywhere.' The other three are genuine defining properties.

questions.q: What is Var(W_t) for standard Brownian motion at time t?
options: Var(W_t) = t²
Var(W_t) = t
Var(W_t) = √t
Var(W_t) = 0
questions.explain: Since W_t − W_0 ~ N(0, t−0) = N(0,t) and W_0=0, Var(W_t) = t exactly — the continuous-time analog of the random walk's Var(S_n) = nσ².

questions.q: Why is a standard Brownian motion path differentiable nowhere, despite being continuous everywhere?
options: Because Brownian motion has discontinuous jumps
Because the increment over a shrinking interval Δt has standard deviation √Δt, so the implied slope (ΔW/Δt) has standard deviation 1/√Δt, which blows up as Δt → 0
Because Brownian motion is not a real-valued process
Because W_0 is not equal to zero
questions.explain: The increment's standard deviation shrinks only as √Δt, slower than Δt itself, so dividing by Δt to approximate a slope produces a quantity whose variability diverges as Δt → 0 — there is no well-defined derivative.

questions.q: What does the quadratic variation of Brownian motion over [0,t] converge to?
options: 0, just as it would for any smooth differentiable function
t, the elapsed time itself — informally written (dW)² = dt
t², the square of the elapsed time
Infinity
questions.explain: Summing squared increments (W_{t_{i+1}} − W_{t_i})² over a fine partition of [0,t] converges to t, not to 0. This nonzero quadratic variation is why stochastic calculus (and Itô's lemma) differs from ordinary calculus.

questions.q: How would you simulate a discretized Brownian motion path over [0,T] with n_steps equal intervals of size dt = T/n_steps?
options: Draw each increment from a Uniform(0,1) distribution and sum them
Draw each increment i.i.d. from N(0, dt) and take the cumulative sum
Set every increment equal to dt exactly, with no randomness
Draw each increment from N(0, dt²) and multiply them together
questions.explain: Each increment W_{t+dt} − W_t should be drawn i.i.d. from N(0, dt) (matching the defining property W_t − W_s ~ N(0, t−s)), and the path is built by cumulatively summing these increments.
